title: Pinch-pot textured salt cellar
subtitle: A small open salt vessel made by pinching, with a pressed-texture exterior
excerpt: A pinch-pot salt cellar is a small, open vessel that sits beside the cooker or on the table for a pinch of salt. This version uses air-dry clay with a stamped or found-texture exterior: sea shell, woven cloth, or cut cork. The form is small enough to dry in under 24 hours.
sourceNotes: Pinch-pot technique derived from first principles: the oldest ceramic form. Salt cellars documented in British domestic pottery from the seventeenth century onward; V&A open-access collection for historical examples.

glossaryTerms.definition: A vessel formed by pressing the thumb into a clay ball and pinching the walls outward between thumb and fingers.
The drying stage where clay holds its shape but is still damp enough to trim and join.
Air-dried but unfired clay. Fragile; the final stage before sealing an air-dry piece.

content.text: The
pinch pot

is the oldest ceramic form: a ball of clay pressed open with the thumb and widened by rotating between finger and thumb. A salt cellar is a natural application: the walls want to be thick enough to hold weight (3 to 4 mm at the base, 4 to 5 mm at the rim) and the opening wide enough for a fingertip. This tutorial uses air-dry clay so no kiln is required, but because the finished cellar will sit near salt and moisture, seal it thoroughly before use.

Add texture to the outside of the pot. Do this while the clay is still soft. This step is optional. Press a piece of woven cloth to leave a grid of tiny squares. Press a cut cork to leave a ring of dots. Press a sea shell flat to leave ridges.
What you'll need

Around 80 g of air-dry clay makes one small salt cellar, roughly 6 cm across and 4 cm tall. A texture object: sea shell, cut cork, woven hessian, or commercial pottery stamp: for pressing the exterior.
Forming the pot
Roll 80 g of clay into a smooth ball between both palms, working out any surface cracks. Press firmly with the thumbs, not just rolling the surface.

Hold the ball in one hand and press the opposite thumb into the centre, stopping 6 mm from the base. Rotate the ball a quarter-turn and pinch: press the thumb outward against two fingertips on the outside wall. The wall should move, not just compress. Each pinch-rotate cycle thins the wall by 1 to 2 mm.

Continue pinching around the full circumference, working upward from the base toward the rim. After one full circuit, rotate the pot 180 degrees and work the same circuit again to even out the thickness. Aim for a wall of 4 mm throughout.
Pat the base flat on the work surface to create a stable foot. Press lightly: you want a flat base, not a thicker one.

Press the texture object firmly into the exterior wall while the clay is still fresh. Work around the full circumference, overlapping each impression slightly so the pattern is continuous. Press straight in and pull straight out: rocking creates smeared edges.
Smooth the rim with a dampened fingertip, rolling it slightly inward to prevent chipping during drying.
Set the pot upright on a smooth tile. If the rim has become uneven, trim it level with the needle tool while the clay is still fresh.
Drying
Leave the salt cellar uncovered at room temperature. Because the walls are thin, it passes through
leather-hard
within four to six hours and reaches
bone-dry
overnight. Check the base: if it feels cooler than the walls it is still drying from the inside. Do not seal until the temperature is even all over.
Finishing

Sand the rim with 400-grit sandpaper, working in a circle. Apply two thin coats of acrylic sealant inside and out, allowing each coat to dry for an hour before the next. Pay particular attention to the interior, where moisture from damp salt could penetrate unsealed clay. The finished cellar is water-resistant, not waterproof: empty it and wipe it dry after each use.
Care

Wipe the interior with a dry cloth between uses. Do not soak in water or run under a tap. If the sealant wears away after heavy use, sand lightly and re-apply two fresh coats. This piece is decorative; salt stored inside it should be used within a week or two rather than left for months, since prolonged humidity can soften the body over time.
Variations

A pinch pot is a ball of clay pressed open with the thumb, then widened by turning between finger and thumb. It is the oldest ceramic form. A salt cellar is a good first pinch pot project. The walls need to be 3 to 4 mm thick at the base and 4 to 5 mm at the rim. The opening needs to be wide enough for a fingertip. This tutorial uses air-dry clay. No kiln is needed. Seal the finished piece well, as it will sit near salt and moisture.
Pinch in paper-clay-air-dry for a stronger, lighter-weight piece with less risk of cracking at the rim.

rows.cause: Walls too thin at the rim; rim dried faster than the base
rows.fix: Keep walls at least 4 mm thick. If a crack appears, dampen the area with a wet brush and smooth closed with a fingertip before it propagates further.

rows.cause: Base not patted flat before drying began
rows.fix: While still leather-hard, set the pot upside down on a flat tile for 30 minutes to let the base flatten under its own weight.

rows.cause: Clay too wet when pressed; texture object rocked rather than pressed straight in
rows.fix: Wait until the clay surface is no longer shiny before impressing. Press the texture object straight in and pull it straight out.
